bead 0.16.0 · spec 0.17.0 · layouts 0xA1 and 0xB1

Bead

One typed contract for teams that call each other in TypeScript, C# and Rust, from a browser, a service or a device behind an MQTT broker.

A service is declared once, in a .proto. beadc generates its typed server and client in each language. A gateway each side offers answers the same procedures in HTTP and JSON, for the teams that do not speak Bead. A specification holds the sides to one behaviour: each plays its conformance files, the Rust side the part it reaches, and the support matrix lists each place where they still differ.

Where Bead stands

Bead is one person’s project, kept at its author’s pace. It has not reached 1.0.0, and it has not run in production. It is not offered as a product to depend on: it is a vision of a company’s own protocol. A team takes it whole and makes it its own, the protocol included: it changes the specification to its needs, and the conformance files and the method keep its implementations in step as it does. That method is in the repository, with its gates, its workflows and its agents’ instructions, so a team can carry it on with an agent.

The ideas, the protocol’s design and the TypeScript side are its author’s. Much of the rest was written by AI agents under the repository’s gates: the other implementations, the generator, and many of the spec’s readings of standards. The idioms of the other languages, and those readings, were checked by the tests, the design rounds and the agents’ reviews. No one with the knowledge to judge them has reviewed Bead’s core, its security or its reading of the standards it follows; a team that takes it reviews it as its own code.

On francisdesjardins.ca, its author tells how Bead is made: the experiment behind that method, and what it shows so far.

Bead in one example

Bead is a binary protocol for calls between a client and a server. A request receives its result or its failure, a subscription its notifications, and the server can call its client in turn. A large payload goes in chunks, and a call can be cancelled on the way. Every envelope opens with the same 8-byte prefix and has no length of its own, so any transport that delimits its messages can carry it. Here is a whole request, byte by byte.

A1layout10REQUEST00no block033 words: 12 bytes00 00 00 03callId 3, odd: the client calls00 02service 200 01procedure 168 69payload: “hi”
  • prefix, the same for every kind
  • the kind’s own
  • an optional block
  • a failure
  • the payload

Once beadc has generated a service’s server and client, what is left to write is the resolvers and the calls, here abridged from examples/hello: 

// the server: its admission hooks, by the names the .proto gives them, and a resolver that asks
// its caller back before it answers
const hello = new HelloServer({ admissions: { greeted } });

hello.on('sayHello', async ({ connectionHandle, payload }, response) => {
  const name =
    payload.name === ''
      ? (
          await hello.command.askName({ question: 'What is your name?' })({ connectionHandle })
        ).name
      : payload.name;

  return response({ greeting: `Hello, ${name}!` });
});
hello.offer(server);

// the client: answers the server's command, calls, and follows a subscription at its own pace
await using client = createWebSocketClient();
const greeter = new HelloClient(client, { windows: { countDown: 1 } });

greeter.on('askName', (_request, response) => {
  return response({ name: 'Ada' });
});
await client.connect({ host: '127.0.0.1', port });

const { greeting } = await greeter.sayHello({ name: '' })(); // 'Hello, Ada!'

await greeter.notifications.countDown({ from: 3 }, async ({ remaining }) => {
  // a window of 1: the next tick waits until this callback settles
})();

The questions a team asks before it adopts Bead, each answered below:

  1. Can our teams, in three languages, share one typed contract?
  2. Can a team that does not adopt Bead still call our services?
  3. What breaks when the contract changes, and how do we know before we deploy?
  4. Which transport for which part of our system?
  5. Does every side behave the same, down to the failures and the timeouts?
  6. When a call fails, how do we see what went by?
  7. How is a call authenticated and authorized, and what is left to us?

Each section gives its gist first, and the longer details are folded under a triangle. After the questions comes the protocol, in detail.

Where Bead differs, and where it does not

Bead does not invent the typed contract, and it is not alone in carrying one to a browser. It differs in four narrow ways.

  • The browser is a full peerOver a WebSocket or plain HTTP, with no translating proxy, a page receives the server’s own calls and answers them, and follows subscriptions at its own pace. Over a WebSocket it also sends large payloads in chunks, under the receiver’s credit.
  • A broker is one more transportOver MQTT 5, and over AMQP 1.0 on the TypeScript and C# sides, both ends keep the API they have over a WebSocket.
  • One credit paces a subscription as it paces a transferA client that asks for it takes notifications only as fast as it handles them. What waits can be kept by key, so a state keeps its latest value.
  • The spec’s conformance files are its executable formEach side plays those files, not a copy of its own, and the Rust side plays the part it reaches.

The architecture guide sets Bead beside gRPC-Web, Connect and SignalR. The other projects’ cells quote or sum up their own pages. What Bead lacks beside them: it is unpublished, and it speaks three languages.

One contract for every team

Write the contract once. beadc generates the code around each call in every language, and the conformance files hold that code to one behaviour. Your team writes the procedures, and what is its own: who may call them, its keys and its deployment.

A team writes the .proto with Bead’s options, a beadc.yaml, the resolvers and the calls. beadc writes the rest, in each language: the typed server and client, the validators, the route table, the OpenAPI document and the HTTP client.

A payload’s rules belong to the contract too, written with protovalidate’s options in the .proto: a payload’s rules shows how.

examples/hello is the same program in TypeScript, C# and Rust. In CI each client calls each server, and every client writes the same lines. To start one outside this repository, the getting-started guide builds a C# server and a TypeScript client from an empty folder.

Generated from a .proto

beadc, the generator, reads a .proto compiled by buf and draws a blueprint from it, a JSON file that describes the API without depending on any language. beadc check judges it by its rules, each refusal at its line and column. Each language’s target then writes its code from it, and beadc breaking holds it to the last release. beadc runs in a Docker image. One contract gives several packages, each with its own selection of procedures. The demo’s Packages tab cuts a blueprint into packages with beadc’s own code.

The way to each language’s code, drawn

Teams that do not speak Bead

A team that does not speak Bead calls the same procedures in HTTP and JSON, through a gateway each side offers. It needs no Bead client: curl, a page’s fetch, or a client generated from the OpenAPI document beadc writes.

The gateway is one more client of its application’s server, through the in-memory transport. Each HTTP exchange draws its own Bead connection, closed when its response ends. What Bead ties to a connection, its session or its subscriptions, thus stays with a single caller: a shared connection would lend the next caller the first one’s session (CWE-441). Its calls go through the server’s router, admission, sessions and rules, like any client’s.

A companion of the specification, spec/transcoding.md, describes it under its own version, 0.7.0. The gateway listens on its own port, localhost by default, or mounts into the application’s web server.

What the wire can do and a gateway does not carry is listed, not hidden: a connection’s session, a command and a stream’s window, each a row of the support matrix’s “Leveled down” (the companion’s §2.5, §2.6 and §8.8). A stream’s resumption has its row there too (§8.3): Server-Sent Events offer it, and a Bead subscription keeps no notification past its end.

A call’s credential is its request’s authorization field. By default, the gateway presents it ELSEWHERE, and the server’s verifier makes of it what the application decides. With its option authorization at bearer-jwt, it presents a Bearer field’s token as a JWT, which the server verifies. It reads no credential from a cookie or a query string.

A call with curl to the gateway of the server with joined transports, on port 8081:

$ curl -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"name":"Ada"}' http://localhost:8081/api/Hello/sayHello
{"greeting":"Hello, Ada!"}

The routes

Each procedure a client calls answers at POST /api/<Service>/<procedure>. It also answers GET when the .proto marks it idempotency_level = NO_SIDE_EFFECTS, the Connect protocol’s rule. Each google.api.http rule of its method also adds a REST route beside the default ones. Those rules are the standard grpc-gateway and Envoy read. An unknown path receives 404, a method refused 405.

The matching, the binding and the OpenAPI document

The path is read raw, with no normalization. When two routes match, a literal goes before *, and * before **. A request binds from its variables, its query string and its body, and a field set twice is refused. A PATCH with no update_mask gets one from its body’s keys, as AIP-134 has it.

beadc writes the route table of each side. It also writes one OpenAPI 3.1.1 document: of the procedures an output’s gateway selects, or of the whole blueprint by default. One blueprint gives the same bytes, whatever writes it. The gateway serves it at /openapi.json, with an etag. A payload’s rules are written there in JSON Schema 2020-12’s words. The detail is in the companion’s §3, §4 and §11.

A message’s JSON

A proto payload is written in protobuf’s JSON mapping. A json payload passes as it is, a text one as text/plain, a raw one as application/octet-stream. The stock protobuf libraries do not agree on that mapping, so Bead has its own reader and writer, on each side. It writes one form: no white space, the members in the order of their field numbers, a map’s entries sorted. In CI, protobuf’s conformance suite plays that mapping on every side through its JSON tests, and each side’s codec through its binary ones.

A failure, a problem

Each failure answers an RFC 9457 problem, application/problem+json. code and scope carry what the wire carries, and detail the failure’s detail. The status depends on where the code arose: what the caller can fix gives a 4xx, what happens between the gateway and its server a 5xx.

StatusWhat raised it
400PAYLOAD_UNDECODABLE of a body, a query string or a variable, or of a json, text or raw request; an application’s failure
401SESSION_REQUIRED, its challenge in www-authenticate
403ACCESS_DENIED
413ENVELOPE_TOO_LARGE, PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE
422PAYLOAD_INVALID, its violations in errors
429CAPACITY_EXCEEDED, retry-after: 1
500PROCEDURE_FAILED, and what is said only between the gateway and its server
501SERVICE_UNKNOWN, PROCEDURE_UNKNOWN
502an answer the gateway could not take; DESTINATION_LOST; LAYOUT_UNSUPPORTED, KIND_UNSUPPORTED; PAYLOAD_UNDECODABLE of a proto request
503DESTINATION_UNREACHABLE, retry-after: 1
504TRANSFER_STALLED, or the call’s timeout, 5 s by default

A PAYLOAD_INVALID gives a 422 whose errors place each violation: pointer into the body, or parameter for a variable of the path or of the query string. The request below calls the route /v1/ruled/{title} of the conformance files’ service. Its body puts from past 10, and its path variable title is past 3 characters. The gateway writes the problem on one line; it is shown indented here. 

POST /v1/ruled/Bead HTTP/1.1
host: localhost
content-type: application/json
content-length: 11

{"from":12}
{
  "code": 52,
  "errors": [
    {
      "bounds": {"lte": 10},
      "detail": "must be less than or equal to 10",
      "fieldPath": "from",
      "pointer": "#/from",
      "ruleId": "int32.lte"
    },
    {
      "bounds": {"max_len": "3"},
      "detail": "must be at most 3 characters",
      "fieldPath": "title",
      "parameter": "title",
      "ruleId": "string.max_len"
    }
  ],
  "scope": "protocol",
  "status": 422,
  "title": "PAYLOAD_INVALID",
  "type": "tag:francisdesjardins.ca,2026:bead/PAYLOAD_INVALID"
}

Notifications, as Server-Sent Events

A request that asks for text/event-stream in its accept opens a subscription. The result goes first, event: result. Each notification follows with no event name, so an EventSource hears it on onmessage. The failure that ends the subscription goes as event: failure. The gateway paces the subscription at the rate the reader takes the events, and a late reader holds the server’s queue, never the gateway’s memory. 

event: result
id: 1
data: {"ticks":2}

id: 2
data: {"remaining":1}

id: 3
data: {}

event: failure
id: 4
data: {"code":2,"scope":"application","status":400,"title":"COUNTED","type":"https://example.com/problems/COUNTED"}
Its gates and its bounds

The gateway judges a request by the HTTP transport’s gates, in the same order. After the origin’s gate, it adds one of Fetch Metadata: a request with no origin whose sec-fetch-site is same-site or cross-site is refused 403, unless it is a GET navigation to /openapi.json or to a procedure marked NO_SIDE_EFFECTS. A call waits 5 s for its answer by default, then receives 504, and no field of the request changes that timeout. A request abandoned closes its connection, and the server cancels its calls.

The client beadc writes

For an output with gateway, beadc also writes a typed client of the default routes of the procedures that gateway selects: over fetch on the TypeScript side, over HttpClient on the C# side, and over hyper on the Rust side. The client reads each problem as a Bead failure, and a stream as an async sequence. The interop calls each side’s gateway with the client of each other side.

Evolving without breaking

A contract changes while older clients still run. beadc breaking says what a change breaks before it ships, and on the wire every byte the layout 0xA1 does not define already has a fate.

Your contract

beadc breaking holds a .proto to its last release and lists what breaks: a procedure deleted, a message switched, an admission tightened, a route shadowed. Under WIRE, a peer built from the earlier release must still talk with one built from the current. Under API, the default, every WIRE rule holds, and code written against the earlier generated API must also still compile and mean the same.

Ids are for life. A service’s id and a procedure’s never change, and the wire carries the id, not the name.

The wire

A peer that does not know a newer version refuses what it cannot read, instead of reading it wrong.

  • A layout to come0xA2 to 0xAF: refused LAYOUT_UNSUPPORTED, the detail saying the layouts read.
  • A kind to come0x17 to 0x7F: reported KIND_UNSUPPORTED.
  • An advisory kind0x80 to 0xFF: ignored, with no error.
  • A credential scheme to come4 to 65,535: read whole; on a request, refused CREDENTIAL_UNSUPPORTED; on a result or a failure, ENVELOPE_MALFORMED.
  • The limitsNothing announces them. What exceeds the other’s limit is refused, never truncated. A failure’s detail alone is cut at its bound, on a character’s boundary.
  • Any other bitA flag its kind does not take, or a kept bit, makes the envelope malformed.

Bead itself

Bead’s versions run on three axes, each moving alone: the layout, the first byte of every envelope; the specification; and the product, one version that the three implementations and beadc share. Before 1.0.0 a minor may break, and the changelog says what each release changes.

The transports

Both ends keep the same API whatever carries the envelopes, so a team picks the transport by where its calls run.

Where the call runsTransportSides
A page or a serviceWebSocketall three
Where WebSocket cannot passHTTP, a long poll for what the server sendsall three
A page and its Web WorkerWeb WorkerTypeScript
Two routers of one processIn memoryall three
One server over several transportsJoinedall three
Devices and servicesMQTT 5all three
Services behind RabbitMQ 4AMQP 1.0TypeScript and C#

In a page or in Node, the TypeScript side depends on no package. A project adds the optional peers it uses: protobuf-es, MQTT.js, rhea or undici. A WebSocket server in Node also takes ws’s WebSocketServer, which its application installs and passes to it.

The same behaviour on every side

The three sides answer to one specification, and to the conformance files that are its executable form: every unit of the spec is cited by a file, or carries the reason none does. Each side plays those files from spec/, the Rust side the part it reaches, and the three call each other in CI. Where they still differ, each difference is a row of the support matrix, with the test that shows it.

TypeScript and C# are at behavioural parity. The Rust side has the parts below, and what it lacks is ahead.

PartTypeScriptC#, on .NET 10Rust
The wireThe envelope, the headers, the failuresThe same, byte for byteThe same, byte for byte, but AMQP 1.0’s messages, ahead with its binding
Above the wireThe routers, the services, sessions and JWTs, a payload’s rules, subscriptions, transfers, relays, debugging and metricsThe same, but a service manager over a router of the application’s own
The transportsWebSocket, HTTP, Web Worker, in memory, a broker over MQTT 5 or AMQP 1.0, and joinedWebSocket, HTTP on Kestrel, in memory, a broker over MQTT 5 or AMQP 1.0, and joinedWebSocket on tungstenite, HTTP on hyper, in memory, a broker over MQTT 5, and joined
The HTTP/JSON gatewayOn node:http, or mounted into a serverOn Kestrel, or mounted by its HttpContextOn hyper, or mounted by its answer

Parity holds down to the field. Where one platform cannot do what another can, the difference either stays between the sides or is leveled, every side keeping to what that platform can. A 64-bit field, a chunk’s offset for instance, is leveled: it stops everywhere at 253 − 1, which a JavaScript number holds exactly. The support matrix keeps each such limit in its “Leveled down” register.

The sides also measure themselves. TypeScript and C# measure the same layers in the same units: the envelope’s codec, a JSON payload, protobuf’s JSON mapping, an echo over HTTP, over WebSocket and in memory, paced notifications and a 20 MiB transfer. Rust measures its codec, its JSON mapping and its echo in memory; its layers on the loopback are ahead. On each release’s branch, CI measures each side against the last release. It runs both trees in turn on one machine and compares them. A regression is read and judged, never a gate.

What each implementation plays

In CI, the three sides call each other over WebSocket, HTTP and MQTT 5, and through their gateways, and the TypeScript and C# sides over AMQP 1.0 too.

The conformance files, in figures
  • The units: 411 for the specification, 185 for debugging and 194 for transcoding, each held by the sha256 fingerprint of its text.
  • The vectors: 474, in 17 groups. They hold the bytes of headers, envelopes and failures, and what a reader refuses of them; a JWT’s verdicts and the credentials refused; a broker’s parcels; the MQTT 5 PUBLISH and the AMQP 1.0 message that carry a parcel, counted to the byte; and the Reason Codes each MQTT 5 acknowledgement names.
  • The conversations: 210, each a script between clients and the interop server, relays included.
  • The transports’ cases: 301, each at a transport’s edge, over HTTP, over WebSocket and over a broker, written byte by byte.
  • The durations: 35 places that take a duration, and what each makes of 19 inputs.
  • The payloads: 184 payloads read and 54 values written, in raw, text, json and proto.
  • A payload’s rules: 180 verdicts and 64 details.
  • Transcoding: 26 templates, 192 readings, 78 writings, 66 bindings, 46 failures, 10 event streams and 99 exchanges.
  • Fuzzing: each suite fuzzes its readers on mutations of the vectors.
The specification first

A behaviour is written in spec/spec.md before it is coded, its MUST and SHOULD in the sense of BCP 14 (RFC 2119, RFC 8174). The conformance files then play it. Where no file can play it, each side that carries it has a twin test, named by one sentence in every language’s case: the TypeScript side’s says at connect that it listens, then listens: a batch heard in order, acknowledged by the next listen is the C# side’s Says_at_connect_that_it_listens_then_listens_a_batch_heard_in_order_acknowledged_by_the_next_listen and the Rust side’s says_at_connect_that_it_listens_then_listens_a_batch_heard_in_order_acknowledged_by_the_next_listen.

Time passed in

Each side takes a call’s timeout, and everything else the specification times, from a clock it is given. A heartbeat runs on the real clock, and so do the bounds of a platform’s own socket, parser and close. spec/clocks.json holds what every side’s test clock does. The TypeScript side’s clock is the part of the globals it calls, so a test gives it a clock it advances by hand, and a timeout fires when the test says so:

On the Rust side, spawning and time go through one module, crate::platform, and the clock alone. Clippy’s disallowed-methods and disallowed-types refuse every other path, so the core also compiles for a browser’s WebAssembly, wasm32-unknown-unknown, which CI checks:

The files do not reach everything. The reviews before each release still find differences between the sides that no file caught, and each is fixed or becomes a row of the support matrix.

What CI holds

  • The conformance files on every side, and the sides calling each other, both ways.
  • Protobuf’s conformance suite, over each side’s JSON mapping and codec.
  • A differential against protovalidate-es, for a payload’s rules.
  • A weekly fuzzing campaign over each side’s parsers, guided by coverage, and coverage floors.
  • Each side’s public surface pinned to its list, and every public name mapped across the languages.

Debugging and observing

Each side tells what goes by: each step of a call, each envelope, each broker parcel, at no cost while no one listens. Its metrics take OpenTelemetry’s RPC vocabulary, in Prometheus’s format. A panel in Chrome’s DevTools shows a page’s calls, even to a server in a Web Worker.

The service manager’s debug event tells each step of a call: tx for a step out, rx for a step in. Each step gives its type, its procedure, its callId, what went out and came in, decoded, and its duration. Each router’s debug tells each envelope, its header copied without its credential. A broker participant’s debug tells its parcels, its link’s transitions, its names and its reports.

With no listener and no registry, a call reads no clock and allocates nothing for debugging: one check per call, one per envelope, one per parcel. A listener that throws never changes a call. Its error goes to the error event, and the call keeps the same outcome and the same bytes on the wire.

A server also says what it holds. gauges() counts, layer by layer, the calls, the transfers, the subscriptions and the sessions. health() draws a verdict from them in the IETF health-check draft’s format: a layer that keeps something for a connection gone is a leak, and fails. Each end-to-end test ends on a server back to zero.

Debugging stays beside the wire, in a companion, spec/debugging.md, under its own version, 0.11.1. A constrained side can leave it out of its build and still conform to the wire.

Bead’s trace is each side’s own. It carries no trace context between peers, so a call that crosses a relay or a gateway is not joined into one distributed trace.

The DevTools extension

A Bead panel in Chrome’s DevTools shows the calls, the envelopes and the metrics of each client a page builds. It also shows the calls a page makes to a server in a Web Worker. The Network panel does not see those messages. The Bead panel also has a Broker view, which follows a broker’s participants and their parcels. A client announces itself to the extension on its own, unless its options say devtools: false. The extension is on the Chrome Web Store, and is built from the repository as well.

What a listener receives

Captured on a WebSocket client: an echo request that succeeds. The listener receives (error, info), and error stays null while the call does not fail. 

// a call's listener: (error, info), for the request echo('hi') that succeeds
null, {
  callId: 3,
  connectionHandle: 'server',
  direction: 'rx',
  duration: 1,
  options: { timeout: 2000 },
  procedureId: 2,
  procedureName: 'echo',
  rx: 'HI',
  serviceId: 1,
  serviceRevision: 1,
  startedAt: 1790700108977,
  tx: 'hi',
  type: 'request',
}
// its outgoing step, at the same start: direction 'tx', duration: undefined, rx: undefined
A failure, a notification, and a router’s envelopes

A failure arrives as error, a FailureError that says who raised it and where. A notification heard is a single step in, with no options and no duration. 

// echo(''): the server answers the procedure's failure 21
FailureError {
  code: 21,
  detail: 'nothing to echo',
  header: { callId: 5, kind: 0x12 },
  origin: 'peer',
  procedureAddress: { procedureId: 2, serviceId: 1 },
  relays: 0,
  scope: 1, // APPLICATION
  side: 'server',
  …
}, {
  direction: 'rx',
  duration: 1,
  options: { timeout: 5000 },
  procedureName: 'echo',
  rx: { code: 21, detail: 'nothing to echo', scope: 1 },
  startedAt: 1790700108978,
  tx: '',
  type: 'request',
  …
}

// a notification heard: one step in, no options, no duration; its start, when it arrives
null, {
  direction: 'rx',
  duration: undefined,
  options: undefined,
  procedureName: 'news',
  rx: 'flash',
  startedAt: 1790700108981,
  tx: undefined,
  type: 'notification',
  …
}

A router’s listener receives each envelope’s header and its connection. Here, the server announces the session on its first RESULT, then the client drops a subscription. 

// the client's router, in order: its connection is always 'server'
{ connectionHandle: 'server', direction: 'tx', header: { callId: 1, kind: 0x10, procedureId: 1, serviceId: 1 } }
{ connectionHandle: 'server', direction: 'rx', header: { callId: 1, credentialScheme: 1, kind: 0x11 } }  // the session announced, OPAQUE
{ connectionHandle: 'server', direction: 'tx', header: { callId: 7, kind: 0x10, opensSubscription: true, procedureId: 4, serviceId: 1 } }
{ connectionHandle: 'server', direction: 'rx', header: { callId: 7, kind: 0x11 } }  // its result, the subscription open
{ connectionHandle: 'server', direction: 'rx', header: { callId: 7, kind: 0x13 } }  // the notification
{ connectionHandle: 'server', direction: 'tx', header: { callId: 7, kind: 0x16 } }  // the subscription dropped

// the server's router names the client's connection
{ connectionHandle: 'type=WS;ip=127.0.0.1;port=57218;ordinal=1', direction: 'rx', header: { callId: 1, … } }

Filtering

filterDebug and filterEnvelopeDebug let through only what a filter keeps. The filter takes the words of the debug package’s DEBUG variable: * for any run of characters, - to leave a name out. It adds three selectors.

Word Keeps
d(rx), d(tx) The events in that direction
t(r), t(n), t(c) The requests, the notifications or the commands
e(failure), e(chunk)… The envelopes of that kind
get*, -getStatus The procedures whose name matches, or all but them 
const filter = () => {
  return process.env['DEBUG_CALLS'];
};

services.on('debug', filterDebug((error, info) => {
  console.log(info.direction, info.procedureName, error);
}, filter));
router.on('debug', filterEnvelopeDebug(({ direction, header }) => {
  console.log(direction, header);
}, filter));

// DEBUG_CALLS="d(rx), t(r|c), e(failure), get*, -getStatus"

Metrics

A metrics registry, createMetricsRegistry(), is given to a router. The router counts at its gates, by service and by procedure, in OpenTelemetry’s RPC vocabulary: the calls that start and those that end, by outcome, on the client’s side and on the server’s. Durations go into gRPC A66’s buckets, from 0 to 100 s. exposition() writes the registry in Prometheus’s text format. The application serves it at /metrics: Bead opens no port. 

const metricsRegistry = createMetricsRegistry();
const server = createServer({ transport }, { metricsRegistry });

// at /metrics, for Prometheus, and a Grafana behind it
const { contentType, text } = metricsRegistry.exposition();
// contentType: 'text/plain; version=0.0.4; charset=utf-8'
An excerpt of an exposition, and what the filter and the metrics guarantee

Nine calls to echo, answered from 0 µs to 100 s plus 1 µs, as spec/metrics.json pins them byte for byte.

  • A filter never fails the call it traces. A direction, a type or a kind that does not exist is refused, never forgotten in silence.
  • Each series exists at 0 as soon as its procedure is declared, so an alert reads it from its start.
  • No label is a connection, a session, a callId or a credential: a peer does not grow the registry.
  • What is under way never reads below 0, and a _sum is written exactly.

Security, plainly

A Bead server keeps itself behind six gates, from the outermost to the innermost. Each gate keeps one thing out, and each refusal but the address’s says why.

The gate What it stops Its refusal
The listening address Another machine, while the server listens on the loopback None: the system refuses the connection
hosts A page that pointed its own name at the server 403 host-refused
origins A page of an origin the server does not name 403 origin-refused
The credential A scheme the server does not take, or a credential that does not hold CREDENTIAL_UNSUPPORTED (36) or SESSION_REQUIRED (32), like a 401
The admission A caller without the right to call this procedure, or one that presented no credential where the procedure needs a session ACCESS_DENIED (33), like a 403, or SESSION_REQUIRED (32), like a 401
The payload’s rules A value the .proto’s rules refuse PAYLOAD_INVALID (52)

A credential, a session

Over HTTP, one says who one is with a session cookie or an Authorization: Bearer token. Bead has an equivalent of each, and a third way.

  • OPAQUE: the token the server drew when a procedure opened the session. It plays the part of a session cookie, tied to its connection.
  • JWT: a signed access token, which each server verifies on the spot, with the keys its application gives it.
  • ELSEWHERE: the credential travels in the transport, and the application’s verifier draws the session from it.

Sessions says how each is verified and how it ends.

Origins and hosts

The threat here is a web page. A page you open can send requests to a server on your machine, and it is your browser that sends them. A WebSocket has no same-origin policy: a page of any site can open one.

origins stops a page of another origin. The browser writes the page’s origin in Origin, and the page cannot change it. The server takes a request with no Origin, of its own origin or of an origin it names, and refuses any other.

hosts stops a page that points its own name at the server, DNS rebinding. Its request then carries its name in Host. The server takes only localhost, the names under .localhost, IP addresses, and the hosts it is told. A server reached by a public name therefore names it.

These two gates keep the server from pages. A program writes the Host and the Origin it wants, and against it stand the listening address and the credential.

TLS and the client’s certificate

A client outside a page takes from its application the authorities it trusts and a certificate with its key, and presents that certificate when its server asks for one. It takes its server’s certificate only when that certificate names the host the client asked for. A page’s TLS is its browser’s.

A client certificate authenticates its client to what terminates TLS, never a request: a call’s credential is still read by the router alone. A server that takes its peer’s certificate as an identity at its admission is ahead.

What to remember

  • EncryptionIt is TLS: wss, https, or a proxy in front of the server.
  • AuthorizationIt falls to each procedure’s admission, which the application writes. beadc check refuses a service that declares none.
  • RateBead bounds what a peer holds of a server, and holds a slow peer to a minimum pace, but caps no rate. Rate limiting falls to the deployment.
  • A stolen tokenA JWT is good for whoever holds it, until its exp plus 60 s. Bead ties it neither to a connection nor to a client’s key.
  • A payload’s meaningBead bounds its size and judges it by its rules. A balance or a right stays with the procedure.
  • Secrets in the logsNothing a side reports carries a credential’s bytes, only its scheme.
How a call presents its credential

Each call carries its own, so two calls of one connection can speak for two people. A bearer credential never leaves the machine in clear. The client’s credential details the default, its withdrawal and the TLS rule.

A relay

A relay terminates each leg and forwards a JWT as it is to the destination of its audience, which verifies it. By default it refuses a call with no credential, or with OPAQUE, so as not to lend its own session to any requester. Relays details it all.

CORS, over HTTP

The HTTP server answers the Fetch Standard’s CORS protocol to the origins origins names, and to no other. It never allows a cookie: no response carries Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, since Bead’s credential is never a cookie. No browser asks CORS for a WebSocket handshake, and origins alone judges it. A proxy in front of the server that appends CORS fields of its own breaks each page listed.

The address it listens on

By default a server listens on localhost, on both loopbacks: 127.0.0.1 then ::1. The network does not reach it (CWE-1327). A container, or a server another machine reaches, listens on 0.0.0.0 or ::, and names its hosts. The address keeps the network out, and hosts the pages of the machine itself.

What TLS does, and Bead does not

Bead’s envelopes and its tokens pass as they are in the transport. Over HTTP in clear, whoever reads the traffic also reads the connection’s token and speaks in its name. Off the machine, HTTP and WebSocket are therefore served under TLS, and the certificates are the deployment’s concern.

The refusal event

A page whose WebSocket is refused sees only a close, 1006, with no reason. Each server therefore tells its application each refusal it judges: the status, the reason, the request’s authority and origin, the client’s address and port. Never the target, nor a token. Behind a proxy, it believes X-Forwarded-For only from the proxies trustedProxies names, and from as many others as unnamedProxies counts. 

transport.on('refusal', ({ address, authority, origin, port, reason, status }) => {
  // 403 host-refused: authority "rebind.example:8080", origin "http://rebind.example:8080",
  // from 127.0.0.1:53114
  console.warn(
    `refused ${status} ${reason}: authority ${JSON.stringify(authority)}, ` +
      `origin ${JSON.stringify(origin)}, from ${address}:${port}`
  );
});
The accessRefused event

Each server also tells each call its router refuses at the credential or at the admission: the stage, the code, the reason in a word, the scheme, what was called, the connection and the address. Never the credential nor its claims: OWASP’s ASVS 5.0 has an authentication or authorization failure logged without its secrets. A JWT refused for exp or kid thus tells the operator whether a clock drifted or a key rotated (§13.12). 

server.router.on(
  'accessRefused',
  ({ address, code, credentialScheme, port, procedureId, reason, serviceId, stage }) => {
    // credential 32 exp: an expired JWT, scheme 2, service 1, procedure 4,
    // from 203.0.113.7:53114
    console.warn(
      `refused ${stage} ${code} ${reason ?? ''}: scheme ${credentialScheme}, ` +
        `${serviceId}/${procedureId}, from ${address}:${port}`
    );
  }
);
What a peer holds of a server

A peer that holds on to a server costs it memory, sockets and time. Each side therefore bounds what a peer holds of it, on the model of HTTP/2 and Kestrel, and each bound can be set.

Bound Default What it holds
maximumAnsweringCalls 64 The calls at once on a connection
maximumConnections, …PerAddress 10,000, 64 A server’s connections, in all and per address
minimumSendBytesPerSecond 240 The pace at which a client takes what waits for it
maximumUnsentBytes 184,551,424 What waits for a WebSocket client’s socket, or for a broker
headersTimeout 30 s The time a request’s head has to come
minimumBodyBytesPerSecond 240 The pace of a body over HTTP, or of an envelope’s parts over a broker
maximumMessageBytes 16,778,240 A WebSocket message; past it, 1009

A client that no longer reads is dropped, and the server reports each drop, naming its bound (§15.12).

To report a vulnerability, SECURITY.md says how.

The protocol, in detail

For the reader who implements a side, audits one, or wants the bytes. Each section follows the specification, spec/spec.md, and references such as §12 point at its sections.

  • 8-byte prefix
  • 23 failure codes
  • 411 units in the spec

Three aims guide each choice. A decoder written by hand reads each field at its place, parsing nothing. A payload is bounded only by the limits of both ends. A refusal says how far the request got.

Choice What Bead does What it gives
The unit Raw bytes behind an 8-byte prefix A codec written by hand, with no serialization framework
The length The envelope carries none of its own: its transport delimits it No ceiling set by a length field; a large payload goes as a transfer, up to 253 − 1 bytes
The fields Fields of 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes, at fixed offsets in 4-byte words Each field read whole at its offset; a flag is one bit to test
The failure Once, in the payload of a FAILURE One place to read it
The codes In blocks of 16, by the stage reached A peer that does not know a code knows its stage
The header 12 bytes for a request, 16 for a chunk or a credit, 8 for the others, before its blocks A size known from the kind, the flags and a credential’s length

Bead takes its ideas from public protocols. The transport delimits the messages, as WebSocket does. An odd or an even callId says who opened the call, as HTTP/2’s streams do. Failure codes go in blocks, as HTTP’s status classes do.

The envelope

Every envelope opens with the same 8-byte prefix. The kind and the flags add fields at fixed offsets, then the payload runs to the end of the message.

In network order, the prefix holds the layout (0xA1), the kind, the flags, the header’s length in 4-byte words, and the callId on 4 bytes. A REQUEST adds its service and its procedure, 2 bytes each.

The flags of the low nibble add blocks, in the order of their bits. DESTINATION (0x02) names a relay’s target in 4 bytes. TRANSFER (0x04) gives a transfer’s total in 8 bytes. CREDENTIAL (0x08) comes last, and it is the only block whose length varies. It is laid out as a TLS extension is: a scheme on 2 bytes, a length on 2, the bytes, then zeros up to the next word. The flags of the high nibble add nothing: SUBSCRIPTION (0x10), PACED (0x20) and MORE (0x40). The bit 0x01 is kept for a block to come, and 0x80 for a flag to come. A header holds 1,020 bytes at most (§2 to §4).

bytes 0-3
layout8kind8flags8length8
bytes 4-7
callId32
bytes 8-11
serviceId16procedureId16
DESTINATION
destinationId32
TRANSFER 1/2
total, high32
TRANSFER 2/2
total, low32
CREDENTIAL 1/5
scheme: OPAQUE16length: 1616
CREDENTIAL 2/5
token, bits 0-3132
CREDENTIAL 3/5
token, bits 32-6332
CREDENTIAL 4/5
token, bits 64-9532
CREDENTIAL 5/5
token, bits 96-12732
Kind Byte Header Its payload
REQUEST 0x10 12 bytes What the procedure receives
RESULT 0x11 8 bytes What the procedure answers
FAILURE 0x12 8 bytes The failure: code, relays, flags, detail
NOTIFICATION 0x13 8 bytes What the subscription announces
CHUNK 0x14 16 bytes, with its offset Bytes of a transfer
CREDIT 0x15 16 bytes, with the end granted None
CANCEL 0x16 8 bytes None

A peer dispatches every envelope it can read by its kind. A REQUEST passes its checks (§9.2), then goes to its procedure. A RESULT or a FAILURE settles the call waiting on that callId. A NOTIFICATION goes to that callId’s subscription. A CHUNK takes its place in its transfer, and a CREDIT moves a transfer being sent, or a paced subscription, forward. A CANCEL makes the peer forget the call. A command, the server’s request to its client, is just a REQUEST on an even callId.

Three more envelopes, byte by byte

A RESULT that announces a session

The flag 0x08 adds the CREDENTIAL block, here OPAQUE and a 16-byte token.

A1layout11RESULT08CREDENTIAL077 words: 28 bytes00 00 00 03callId 3: the same request00 01scheme: OPAQUE00 10length: 169F 3C 51 … 0Bthe token, 16 bytes48 49payload: “HI”

A REQUEST that opens a subscription

The flag 0x10 adds no block: the header stays at 3 words.

A1layout10REQUEST10SUBSCRIPTION033 words: 12 bytes00 00 00 07callId 7: the subscription’s00 02service 200 05procedure 57B 7Dpayload

A NOTIFICATION

It carries the callId of the request that subscribed.

A1layout13NOTIFICATION00no block022 words: 8 bytes00 00 00 07callId 7: the subscription’s7B 22 … 7Dpayload

The callId pairs everything

Every answer, notification, chunk, credit or cancel carries its call’s callId. An odd callId comes from a call the client opened, an even one from a call the server opened. The two sides thus draw from two separate halves, and the server can call its client too. Such a call is a command.

Each side walks through its half of the callIds, about 231, skipping those in use or reserved. At 10,000 calls a second, a lap takes two and a half days. When every one is taken, the call fails on the spot with CAPACITY_EXCEEDED.

By default, at most 64 of a peer’s calls wait for their answer at once on a connection: maximumAnsweringCalls. HTTP/2 bounds the streams a peer opens the same way. Nothing announces this number: both ends set it alike. The requester keeps to it. The receiver refuses one more request with CAPACITY_EXCEEDED once its header reads, before it looks at its route, its credential or its payload (§9.2). A resolver that still runs once its call was answered or cancelled counts until it settles. Together, the calls being answered and those resolvers never pass twice the bound. So a peer that cancels every request it sends never has more resolvers run than that.

An answer goes once, and only while its call is open. One that arrives after a cancel or a close goes nowhere, so that it never settles someone else’s call.

A failure travels once

A failure is the payload of a FAILURE, and nowhere else. It holds a 2-byte code, the number of relays it crossed, a byte of flags, then a readable detail in UTF-8.

The flags’ bit 0x01 says the code belongs to the procedure, so a service’s code 19 never passes for PROCEDURE_UNKNOWN. The detail holds 1,024 bytes at most by default, maximumDetailBytes. A failure that answers a side’s own error, such as a resolver that throws, carries no detail. The error stays with that side, which reports it to its application.

A1layout12FAILURE00no block022 words: 8 bytes00 00 00 05callId 500 15code 21000 relays01APPLICATION65 6D 70 74 79detail: “empty”

The protocol’s codes go in blocks of 16, by the stage reached: the envelope, the route, the admission, the payload, the procedure. A peer that does not know a code knows its stage at least. Each failure meets one of five fates. A code marked with several meets one of them, according to the side that raises it and what it refuses.

  • answeredsent to the peer, on the request’s callId
  • reportedraised locally, never sent
  • rejectedthe call fails before it goes
  • endedthe requester ends its call with it, on an answer it cannot take
  • gateanswered, ended, dropped in silence or reported, by what the gate finds
CodeNameStageFateWhen
1ENVELOPE_MALFORMEDenvelopegateThe bytes do not form an envelope this layout reads, or an envelope that reads comes where none can, such as a REQUEST or a CANCEL of the receiver’s own parity, or a REQUEST on an open callId.
2LAYOUT_UNSUPPORTEDenvelopegateA layout to come, 0xA2 to 0xAF; the detail says the ones read.
3KIND_UNSUPPORTEDenvelopereportedA kind to come, 0x17 to 0x7F; a NOTIFICATION a server received, or a credit of notifications a client received.
4ENVELOPE_TOO_LARGEenvelopegateA request or a result past chunkBytes, whole or an opening, or another envelope past maximumEnvelopeBytes.
16DESTINATION_UNKNOWNrouteansweredA destination the relay does not have, or a peer that relays nothing.
17DESTINATION_UNREACHABLErouteanswered rejectedThe request could not leave, so nothing was tried: its destination is gone, its transport cannot carry its credential, or another error stopped it before it went.
18SERVICE_UNKNOWNrouteansweredNo procedure is registered for this service.
19PROCEDURE_UNKNOWNrouteansweredThe service exists, not the procedure.
20CALL_UNKNOWNroutereportedA RESULT, a FAILURE or a CHUNK no call awaits.
21SUBSCRIPTION_UNKNOWNroutereportedA NOTIFICATION under no subscription.
22SUBSCRIPTION_UNSUPPORTEDrouteansweredA subscription on a path with no notification: a relay, an HTTP connection that does not listen.
32SESSION_REQUIREDadmissionanswered rejectedThe credential does not hold, or the procedure wants a session the call lacks; also sent when a session ends.
33ACCESS_DENIEDadmissionansweredThe admission refuses the call, on its header and its session.
34PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGEadmissionanswered reported rejected endedThe payload, or a transfer’s total, is past its procedure’s or its router’s limit, 16 MiB by default.
35CAPACITY_EXCEEDEDadmissionanswered rejected endedToo many calls at once, no free callId left, or a full queue or budget.
36CREDENTIAL_UNSUPPORTEDadmissionansweredA credential scheme this peer does not take; the detail names its own.
48CHUNK_INVALIDpayloadanswered endedA chunk outside the rules: empty, misplaced, of the wrong size or past the total.
49CREDIT_EXCEEDEDpayloadanswered reported endedA chunk past the credit granted.
50PAYLOAD_UNDECODABLEpayloadanswered reported endedThe procedure’s codec refuses the payload.
51TRANSFER_STALLEDpayloadansweredNothing came for a transfer for 30 s, by default.
52PAYLOAD_INVALIDpayloadanswered rejectedThe payload reads, but breaks a rule of its message.
64PROCEDURE_FAILEDprocedureansweredThe procedure, its admission or a credential’s verifier failed, a rule could not judge, or the result does not write or is too large to go.
65DESTINATION_LOSTprocedureansweredThe relay lost its destination after sending: the procedure may have run.

In the code

On the TypeScript side, the requester receives a FailureError: isProtocol tests a code of the protocol, isApplication a code of the procedure. The C# side’s FailureException and the Rust side’s Failure ask the same. 

import { FailureError, ProtocolCode } from '@francisdesjardins/bead/client';
import { violationsOf } from '@francisdesjardins/bead/service';

try {
  await echo('')();
} catch (reason) {
  const failure = reason instanceof FailureError ? reason : undefined;

  if (failure?.isApplication(21)) {
    // the procedure's own code 21: it refuses an empty text
  } else if (failure?.isProtocol(ProtocolCode.SESSION_REQUIRED)) {
    // the protocol's code 32: open a session, or renew its credential, then call again
  } else if (failure?.isProtocol(ProtocolCode.PAYLOAD_INVALID)) {
    // code 52: each violation names its field and its rule, more counts those left out
    const { more, violations } = violationsOf(failure);
  }
}

What does not read

An envelope that does not read has no callId to trust. Answering it at random could settle someone else’s call, so everything goes through one gate (§9.6).

A REQUEST whose prefix reads, of the peer’s parity and on a free callId, receives a FAILURE on that callId. A RESULT or a FAILURE of the layout 0xA1 that does not read fails the call waiting on it, and the peer receives a CANCEL. A CHUNK of that layout that does not read ends its transfer with CHUNK_INVALID. What arrives late, on a reserved callId or for a transfer already ended, is dropped in silence. Everything else is reported locally, never answered.

A payload’s rules

A request must often hold more than its encoding says: a count of 10 at most, a name of 1 to 63 characters. Those rules are written in the .proto with protovalidate’s options, the protobuf ecosystem’s standard. beadc compiles them into native validators, in TypeScript, in C# and in Rust. 

import "buf/validate/validate.proto";

// Where the count starts, 10 at most.
message CountDownRequest {
  int32 from = 1 [(buf.validate.field).int32.lte = 10];
}

The server judges each request once its payload is read, before its resolver. A request its rules refuse receives PAYLOAD_INVALID (52), and its resolver never sees it. A client can also judge its value before sending, with the validates option: the call then fails on the spot, with the same code and the same detail. The rules judge the payload alone. A name already taken, a balance or a right stay with the resolver, which answers a failure of its procedure.

A PAYLOAD_INVALID FAILURE

The detail carries one line a violation, then a line that closes.

A1layout12FAILURE00no block022 words: 8 bytes00 00 00 09callId 900 34code 52000 relays00PROTOCOL7B 22 62 6F …detail: {"bo…, one violation a line0A 7B 22 6D …then {"more":0}
{"bounds":{"lte":10},"fieldPath":"from","message":"must be less than or equal to 10","ruleId":"int32.lte"}
{"more":0}

Each line is a JSON object in RFC 8785’s canonical form: the field’s path, the rule’s id as protovalidate names it, its bounds and its message. The last line counts the violations left out, {"more":N}, or says the side stopped at the first, {"stopped":true}. The offending value never travels, since it may be a secret. A map’s key is the one exception: the path names an entry by its key, 64 bytes of it at most (§18.4).

What beadc compiles, and how a pattern is judged

beadc compiles required and ignore; a constant, on any scalar or an enum; a number’s bounds and a float’s finiteness; a list of values, for a number, a string or an enum; the lengths, prefix, suffix and contents of a string or of bytes, and a string’s pattern; an enum’s defined values; a list’s and a map’s rules; and oneof. It refuses any other rule with VALIDATE_RULE_UNSUPPORTED, CEL and a pattern of bytes among them. It ignores none: a rule written and not played would let through what a protovalidate server refuses. Rules in CEL are ahead, then the rest of the rules it refuses.

A pattern follows RE2’s syntax and is judged in linear time, with no backtracking (CWE-1333). beadc builds its automaton ahead, from its own Unicode tables, and each validator reads one cell a character. A pattern whose table would pass 16,384 cells is refused, with VALIDATE_PATTERN_LARGE. Violations follow an order Bead fixes, field by field. The order, the paths and the detail’s format are in §18.

Cancel

A requester that gives up on a call tells the peer with a CANCEL, 8 bytes on the call’s callId. A CANCEL is never answered (§10).

A1layout16CANCEL00no block022 words: 8 bytes00 00 00 05callId 5: the call given up

It sends one when its timeout expires, when its signal aborts it, or when it drops a subscription. The other end forgets the call, undoes the subscription and aborts its resolver’s signal. The requester then reserves the callId for the call’s timeout, 5 s if it had none, and drops what arrives late on it. It is HTTP/2’s RST_STREAM, kept to the requester. The side that answers ends a call with a FAILURE, which carries a code, and so needs no CANCEL.

Subscriptions

A subscription is a call left open. Its request carries the SUBSCRIPTION flag, and the server then notifies under its callId (§11).

The request states its intent, as a CoAP GET registers only with its Observe option. An ordinary request to the same procedure subscribes to nothing. The client listens on the callId before it sends the request, so a notification that arrives before the RESULT is heard. The subscription ends at an unsubscribe, a cancel, the connection’s close, its session’s end, or on a failure the application chooses. A connection holds one subscription per procedure and per session.

At the client’s pace

With PACED beside SUBSCRIPTION, the server sends only the notifications the client has granted. The client grants as its callbacks finish, an asynchronous one once its work is done. With a window of one, it grants the next notification once they are done with the previous one. With a wider window, it grants as far as the window reaches past what they finished, and grants again at half the window. It grants with a CREDIT that carries PACED. That credit counts notifications, as RSocket’s REQUEST_N does. But it is absolute, as a transfer’s credit is.

Past its credit, a notification waits in a queue. The server can give it a key. A notification of the same key replaces the one waiting, so an entity’s state keeps only its latest value: forty-five changes to an article, while a callback fetches its data, arrive as two notifications. Without a key, every event is kept, in order. A full queue, 64 notifications or 1 MiB by default, ends the subscription with CAPACITY_EXCEEDED. Nothing is lost in silence: the client subscribes again and reads the state anew.

The two envelopes of a paced subscription

A REQUEST that opens a paced subscription

The request itself grants the first notification.

A1layout10REQUEST30SUBSCRIPTION and PACED033 words: 12 bytes00 00 00 07callId 7: the subscription’s00 02service 200 05procedure 57B 7Dpayload

A CREDIT of notifications

Two notifications sent at most, the first one handled.

A1layout15CREDIT20PACED: notifications044 words: 16 bytes00 00 00 07callId 7: the subscription’s00 00 00 00 00 00 00 02two sent at most

Sessions

A session is what a call runs in: an identifier, data the admission and the procedure read, and an end. Each call runs in the session its credential leads it to (§13).

There are two kinds. A connection’s session opens by a request, a login procedure for instance, and the server keeps it with a 128-bit token drawn at random. A credential’s session is what a verifier draws from a JWT, or from a credential the transport carries. A call without a credential runs in its connection’s session, if there is one.

The server announces the connection’s session in the CREDENTIAL block of a RESULT or a FAILURE, and only when it changes: OPAQUE and its token when it opens, NONE when it ends. The client presents it only on the call that asks for it. When a session ends and the connection stays, each subscription it bounded receives SESSION_REQUIRED.

A request’s credential

A request presents a credential in its CREDENTIAL block. Its scheme names a format, as HTTP names an authentication scheme: a peer knows what the bytes are without reading them.

Scheme Name Its bytes On a request
0 NONE None Malformed; on an answer, the session has ended
1 OPAQUE A session’s token, 16 bytes Its connection’s session, if the token is that session’s
2 JWT A signed access token (RFC 9068) The session its claims carry, once verified
3 ELSEWHERE None: the transport carries the credential The session the application’s verifier draws from it
4 and up to come Those of a format to come Read, then refused CREDENTIAL_UNSUPPORTED
Two session envelopes, byte by byte

A REQUEST that presents a JWT

The block holds its scheme, its length, then the token, padded with zeros to the word.

A1layout10REQUEST08CREDENTIAL4F79 words: 316 bytes00 00 00 03callId 300 02service 200 01procedure 100 02scheme: JWT01 2Alength: 29865 79 4A …the token: eyJ…, 298 bytes00 00padding to the word68 69payload: “hi”

A FAILURE that announces the end

NONE has no bytes: the block takes 4.

A1layout12FAILURE08CREDENTIAL033 words: 12 bytes00 00 00 05callId 5: the subscription00 00scheme: NONE00 00length: 000 20code 32000 relays00PROTOCOL

The call’s session

The server judges the credential, then the admission, on the header alone. A scheme it does not take receives CREDENTIAL_UNSUPPORTED (36), and the detail names those it takes, as a 401 names them in WWW-Authenticate. A credential that does not hold receives SESSION_REQUIRED (32), whatever the procedure wants, as an invalid bearer token receives a 401. A verifier that fails gives PROCEDURE_FAILED. Last, the admission decides on the call’s session, which the resolver then receives.

A procedure never receives its call’s bearer credential. The token goes only to the verifier and, through a relay, to the destination. It is a gateway’s model: the one that verifies a token does not hand it to the code it serves.

A JWT, verified one way

A JWT is an access token of RFC 9068’s profile, and every side verifies it the same way, as RFC 8725 recommends. Its typ is at+jwt, or application/at+jwt, which rules out an identity token from the same issuer. Its key is one of those the application gives, each with its issuer and a single algorithm, ES256 or HS256. Its iss must be that key’s issuer, its exp must hold with 60 s of leeway, and its aud must name the peer’s audience. A token never chooses its own key: jwk, jku, x5u and x5c are never read. Its session is named by its issuer and its sid, or else its sub.

A key set, besides the keys

An application can give a key set for some issuers. Bead asks for it when no known key carries the token’s kid, at most once a minute per issuer, so that no peer has it queried at will. The keys received hold for ten minutes. By default, at most 64 calls of one issuer wait for its next ask, then the next call receives CAPACITY_EXCEEDED; a call that waits on an ask under way is never counted. Bead fetches nothing by itself: the function that brings the keys belongs to the application (§13.9).

A credential’s session ending

A JWT’s session ends at its exp plus 60 s. That of a credential the transport carries ends when its verifier says so. The server keeps it only while it bounds a subscription, and a renewed token of the same identifier pushes its end back. At its end, each subscription receives SESSION_REQUIRED. The application can also end it by its identifier, endSession, or end all of an issuer’s whose key leaked, endSessionsOf. It is no revocation: a token still valid opens the session again.

The client’s credential

A client presents a default credential, given in its options, or a credential of a call’s own. A call can also present none. ELSEWHERE leaves the credential to the transport: the Authorization field of each POST over HTTP, that of the handshake of a WebSocket client outside a browser, the parcel that carries a request over a broker, or what an in-memory client hands with each request.

When a call that presented the default receives SESSION_REQUIRED, the client withdraws that default and tells the application, credentialWithdrawn. Until the application gives a new one, each call that would present it fails before it goes. No call thus falls in silence into another session. A failure that ends a subscription already answered withdraws nothing, since the credential may still hold. For the same reason, an admission answers ACCESS_DENIED, never SESSION_REQUIRED, to a call that presented a credential.

A bearer credential leaves the machine only under TLS (RFC 6750 §5.3): wss, https, or a broker that each peer reaches under TLS. On the machine, the loopback, a Web Worker or a router of the same process are enough. The loopback is judged by the host the client names, never by what that name resolves to. A client connects a localhost name to the loopback itself, asking no resolver, and a host on the loopback through no proxy. A page leaves that connect to its browser, and Node without undici to its platform. Elsewhere, the call fails before it goes with DESTINATION_UNREACHABLE, and the credential stays. A server behind a TLS proxy declares itself secure by the secure option.

Transfers

A payload whose envelope would exceed one chunk, 1 MiB by default, goes as a transfer. It moves forward chunk by chunk, at the pace of the credit its receiver grants, while the other calls go on (§12).

The REQUEST or the RESULT that opens the transfer carries the TRANSFER block, which holds the total on 8 bytes. The payload’s first bytes follow, sent with no credit. The receiver answers with a CREDIT: the offset below which the sender may send. This credit is absolute, like QUIC’s MAX_STREAM_DATA, so a credit repeated or late never grants too much. The receiver grants a window of 4 MiB, renewed at its half.

The sender sends CHUNKs, each with its offset on 8 bytes and MORE on all but the last. Each chunk is exactly full, but the last. The receiver places them in any order, drops what it already has, then hands the whole payload to the procedure or to the requester. A transfer of 20 MiB thus goes as an opening, nineteen full chunks and a last one of 324 bytes.

A transfer is refused before its mass goes by. Its opening passes the route, the credential, the admission and the limits before a single byte is granted. By default, a receiver takes four transfers at once per connection, and 256 MiB for all it receives, on all its connections.

The requester stops a transfer with a CANCEL. The side that answers stops it with a FAILURE: TRANSFER_STALLED after 30 s with nothing, CHUNK_INVALID or CREDIT_EXCEEDED for a chunk outside the rules. A NOTIFICATION, a FAILURE and the result of a call that opens a subscription are never split.

A 20 MiB transfer, byte by byte

The opening

The flag 0x04 adds the total: the header grows to 5 words.

A1layout14CHUNK00no MORE: the last044 words: 16 bytes00 00 00 07callId 700 00 00 00 01 3F FE BCfrom 20,971,196…324 bytes: the total reached
The limits, and what a transport owes Bead

Nothing announces the limits: both ends of a connection set them alike, but the last row’s, which each side sets for itself (§12.2, §15.12).

Limit Default What it bounds
maximumEnvelopeBytes 16,778,240 Any envelope other than a request or a result
chunkBytes 1,048,576 A request or a result, whole or a transfer’s opening, and a chunk within its transfer
windowBytes 4,194,304 The lead a receiver grants
maximumPayloadBytes 16,777,216 A payload; a procedure can tighten it
bufferedBytesBudget 268,435,456 What a side reserves for the transfers it receives
maximumTransfers 4 The transfers received at once on a connection
maximumChunkRuns 1,024 The runs of bytes apart a transfer holds before it is whole
transferInactivityTimeout 30,000 ms The wait for the next chunk or credit
maximumDetailBytes 1,024 A failure’s detail
maximumAnsweringCalls 64 The calls of a peer that wait for their answer at once on a connection
maximumUntakenEnvelopes, maximumUntakenBytes 64, 1,048,576 What a router has not yet taken of one connection. Reaching either bound pauses that connection until each count is back at half.

The transport delimits its messages, carries both directions and delivers each envelope once, in order. Knowing whether a connection lives is its job too: no envelope of Bead’s is a ping. WebSocket does all of it (§1.3, §15.1 to §15.3). HTTP keeps no order between a client’s exchanges, so a CANCEL may come before its REQUEST (§15.1, §15.5). Over a broker, Bead keeps its own heartbeat (§15.21).

Relays

A server can relay a request to a destination registered with it, as a gateway does for what sits behind it. The requester chooses the destination by 4 bytes, the DESTINATION block of its request (§14).

The relay terminates each leg. Leg A runs from the requester to the relay, leg B from the relay to the destination, and each has its callIds, its limits and its session. Only the payload’s bytes cross, undecoded, with the credential the relay forwards and the answer. Each refusal falls at the opening, and a CANCEL on leg A cancels leg B.

The relay forwards a bearer credential, and the destination verifies it. A destination is registered with the audience it verifies, or with none. That audience names it as RFC 8707 names a resource for a token. A destination registered with none takes no bearer credential. By default, the relay’s admission, requireCredential, admits only a credential it can forward. A call with no credential, or with OPAQUE, receives ACCESS_DENIED. Otherwise all these requesters would share leg B’s session, and the relay would lend its own authority (CWE-441). A relay that shares says so in its code: a beforeRoute that checks the destination against the requester’s session, or shareLegBSession.

Leg B Leg A answers
A result, or the destination’s failure That result, or that failure counted one relay more
A limit of leg B’s, a payload or a capacity, before its transport has the request That refusal, the relay’s own
Any other error before its transport has the request DESTINATION_UNREACHABLE (17): nothing was tried
An error after, the connection lost for instance DESTINATION_LOST (65): the procedure may have run

Bead’s gateway answers these two codes with 503 and 502, as an HTTP gateway does. gRPC’s retry rules turn on the same difference: whether the procedure may have run.

What a relay does not do, and what its requesters share

A relay carries no subscription: it refuses to open one with SUBSCRIPTION_UNSUPPORTED. It forms no chain, since leg B names no destination. Its failures name no address behind it. A relay that carries a subscription is ahead.

All of a relay’s requesters share its leg B: one space of callIds, the same 64 calls at once, the same capacity for transfers. So the relay’s admission, which sees the procedure and the destination, checks the rights. By default, the relay does not verify a JWT it forwards, so a forged token learns which destinations exist before the destination refuses it. With the verifies option, the relay verifies the token itself, from its first step.

A destination a connection carries dies with it. It stays registered, unreachable, until the application removes it, or registers the newcomer in its place, replaces.

Over HTTP

Over WebSocket, each envelope is a binary message, in both directions. HTTP serves where WebSocket cannot pass. It keeps no connection, so the transport draws one, and each POST carries an envelope (§15.4 to §15.12).

Where its platform lets it, each end of a WebSocket sends a PING on a connection silent for 30 s, and drops it if no pong echoes the ping. So a peer gone without a word is dropped. The global WebSocket, a page’s or Node’s, sends none, and the server’s pings stand for it. A message past maximumMessageBytes closes the connection with code 1009 (RFC 6455).

A POST with no body connects. The server answers 201 with a 16-byte token in the bead-connection-token field, which each later exchange presents, and a DELETE ends the connection. The router, the sessions and the relays see a connection there as over a socket. Each envelope has the type application/prs.bead. The transport reads only its layout, its kind and its callId, at the prefix’s fixed offsets, to hand each answer to its request’s exchange.

The server marks each of its refusals in the bead-refusal field, and only a marked refusal fails the send beyond doubt: nothing was tried. Any other status, a gateway’s 502 for instance, may have come after the request ran, and counts as an exchange lost. A relay thus always tells DESTINATION_UNREACHABLE from DESTINATION_LOST. A client follows no redirect: it would carry the connection’s token where no one judged it.

A call that presents ELSEWHERE carries its credential in the Authorization field of its POST, so a token is renewed without reconnecting. The server takes only the hosts and the origins it knows: security explains it.

What the server sends of its own

A notification, a command or a relayed request has no exchange to go to. They wait, numbered, in the connection’s outbox. The client listens with a GET /bead the server holds until something arrives, 30 s at most. The server then reports a batch, each envelope preceded by its length on 4 bytes. The next listen acknowledges what was heard by its bead-after field, and the rest comes again.

A listen lost resumes where it was, at once, then after 1, 2, 4 s and up to 30, each wait drawn at random. A brief cut costs nothing: the same connection, its session, its subscriptions, and all that arrived meanwhile, in order. It is a long poll (RFC 6202): no heartbeat, and nothing an intermediary buffers.

A client that does not listen receives no subscription, no command and no relayed request. HTTP carries no transfer: a request’s body arrives before its response goes, and no credit could come back. Under TLS, the server serves HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 on one port.

A request’s timeouts, and WebSocket’s handshake

A request’s head must come whole within 30 s, headersTimeout, or the server answers 408, unmarked. A body must come at 240 bytes a second at least, past a grace of 5 s, or it receives 408 too-slow. A field that holds a control character other than a tab, or a byte past ASCII, is refused before anything else, 400 unmarked over HTTP/1.1 (§15.12).

WebSocket’s handshake is an HTTP request. The WebSocket server judges it by its own hosts and origins, under the same rules, and bounds its connections as an HTTP server does. A handshake without Origin, a client’s outside a browser, carries its Authorization beside each envelope of its connection. A page’s carries none, since its browser adds its user’s own authentication to it, as it adds cookies. A page therefore presents a JWT.

In memory, and several transports

The in-memory transport joins a client’s router and a server’s within one process. The joined transport gives a server its connections from several transports at once (§15.13, §15.14).

In memory, each envelope is copied as it leaves, then delivered whole, once, in order, at a later turn. The transport carries a credential beside a request, as Authorization does over HTTP. It never leaves the process, so both its ends are secure. Each side plays its conformance conversations through a pair of this transport.

The joined transport gives one router, one admission, one handling of sessions, and each service offered once, whatever the call’s transport. It is joinTransports on the TypeScript side, and JoinedServerTransport on the C# and Rust sides. Each connection stays its transport’s. That is how the HTTP/JSON gateway calls its application’s server. Each transport takes the procedures it is given, every one by default. A request to any other is answered as one to no procedure, SERVICE_UNKNOWN or PROCEDURE_UNKNOWN, before its credential is read (§9.11). 

const webSocket = createWebSocketTransportServer({ WebSocketServer });
const memory = createMemoryTransportServer();
const server = createServer({ transport: joinTransports([webSocket, memory]) });

offerHello(server);

// what beadc generates: the route table, the document, the problem types' base
const gateway = createHTTPGateway({
  createServer: (listener) => {
    return createNodeServer(listener);
  },
  document: OPENAPI_DOCUMENT,
  problemTypes: HTTP_PROBLEM_TYPES,
  routes: HTTP_ROUTES,
  transport: memory,
});

await memory.start();
await webSocket.start({ port: 8080 });
await gateway.start({ port: 8081 }); // localhost: both loopbacks

Over a broker

A topic-based publish/subscribe broker is one more transport, and Bead never becomes a network of its own there. Each side holds its core, an in-memory broker for tests, and its bindings: MQTT 5 on every side, and AMQP 1.0 on RabbitMQ 4 for the TypeScript and C# sides (§15.16 to §15.38).

A participant is a side’s link to its broker. Its identifier is the identity the broker authenticates, and its inbox, the topic bead/i/<id>, receives all that comes to it. A server serves a name, bead/s/<name>, alone or in a group of participants that share it. MQTT 5 writes these topics with slashes. AMQP 1.0 writes them with dots, bead.i.<id> and bead.s.<name>.

A broker often joins services and devices already. Bead adds what topics alone lack: calls with their answers and their failures, cancel, each client’s pace and transfers under credit.

A connection is placed once, at its opening, and named by its two ends, as a TCP connection is by two sockets. The client publishes an OPEN to the server’s name. The broker delivers it to a single member of the group, which answers an ACCEPT to the client’s inbox. The client confirms with a PING, the third leg, like that of TCP’s handshake. From then on, everything goes from inbox to inbox.

Each envelope travels in a parcel, with a 28-byte header of layout 0xB1. Each end numbers what it sends. A copy the broker delivered twice is dropped before the router, and a loss brings the connection down. An envelope too large for the peer’s inbox goes in parts. Bead keeps its own rules on top: a subscription’s credit, a request’s credential, sent to the server alone, and a heartbeat on a silent connection.

The two bindings, MQTT 5 and AMQP 1.0

Over MQTT 5

Each participant is a clean link, which the broker does not keep past its connection: Clean Start and a session that expires at 0. Each parcel is a PUBLISH at QoS 1, or at QoS 0 on a link set to deliver at most once. A name a group serves is a shared subscription, $share/<name>/bead/s/<name>. Each packet is counted to the byte under each end’s maximum size. A participant’s will announces its departure to the peers. The TypeScript side goes through MQTT.js, and the C# side through MQTTnet. The Rust side goes through a client of its own, the feature mqtt of its core. A link runs over TCP, TLS or a WebSocket. All three sides are played against Mosquitto over TCP and over a WebSocket, and under TLS against a scripted peer. Mosquitto under TLS is ahead.

Over AMQP 1.0

The binding targets RabbitMQ 4. Each link is a fresh connection, and its inbox an exclusive queue that ends with it. The deployment provisions each name’s queue, and the broker delivers each of its messages to a single member. Each message follows a single profile, counted to the byte. AMQP 1.0 has no will: Bead’s heartbeat alone says a peer went quiet. The TypeScript side goes through rhea, the C# side through AMQPNetLite, and both are played against RabbitMQ 4. No page reaches an AMQP 1.0 broker.

In both cases, a deployment’s broker authenticates each link, by a password or a TLS client certificate, and its access control lets a participant alone read its inbox.

What is ahead

The first four come in this order, the others in no set order. The decisions’ index lists the rest.

  • Rust’s AMQP 1.0Its binding over AMQP 1.0, by a decision of its own.
  • Rules in CELThe rules written in CEL, a subset beadc compiles into each side, then the rest of the rules it refuses, a string’s well-known formats among them.
  • The close codeWhat the peer said as it closed a connection, carried on close, on every transport.
  • A relay that carries a subscriptionWhat a page needs across a broker.
  • Rust’s service managerA service manager over a router of the application’s own, as the TypeScript and C# sides have.
  • The core in a pageThe C# and Rust sides in a page and in a worker, with the DevTools extension’s hook.
  • More conformanceThe client part over HTTP and WebSocket, a relay across languages, and one corpus read alike by every side’s parsers.
  • A connection’s ageA graceful drain of long-lived connections, as HTTP/2’s GOAWAY drains one.
  • DevTools on FirefoxThe extension on a second browser.
  • A counted call’s costOn each side, a counted call measured against one that is not. This measure comes beside the benches’ own.
  • A constrained C sideDebugging left out of its build by its switches.
  • A peer’s certificate as its identityA server that takes its peer’s certificate as an identity at its admission.
  • PublicationThe packages on npm, NuGet and crates.io, and beadc’s image.

In the code

Bead lives in the router, the middle layer. The transport below moves the envelopes and reads no more of one than its prefix. The services above call and answer without seeing a byte.

The wire’s code

Ten files of the TypeScript side write and read Bead, with no dependency. The prefix reads at fixed offsets, before anything else of the envelope:

And a header is written field by field, each at its offset:

Each of the ten, on GitHub:

  • constants.tsLayouts, kinds, flags, schemes, codes, limits
  • header.tsThe header: written and read at fixed offsets
  • envelope.tsThe whole envelope, and a failure’s record
  • transfer.tsTransfers: the chunks sent, placed, and the credit
  • identifiers.tsThe callIds and the session tokens
  • errors.tsFailureError: a failure received, readable
  • violations.tsA PAYLOAD_INVALID’s violations: written as lines of JSON, read back

  • amqp-messages.tsAn AMQP 1.0 message counted to the byte, its profile, its topics and its addresses

Open the demo Getting started The source on GitHub

The name comes from Baily’s beads, the points of light that break through at the Moon’s edge during an eclipse. It reads another way too: each envelope a bead, strung on its connection, in order, at the pace of the one who receives.
